title: Trump’s China rivalry and “AI race” delusion may endanger US, experts say
gist: Ahead of a Trump–Xi summit, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent touted a US-China AI safety notification channel that experts call superficial because it lacks technical staff, while China has not publicly acknowledged it. Experts argue the US 'AI race' framing is flawed: frontier leads last only months, Chinese open models are winning global adoption, and broad export controls and deregulation may undermine safety cooperation.

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the US and China discussed an AI safety notification mechanism letting either side send alerts when its AI systems pose threats or behave unpredictably, but China has not publicly acknowledged it.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: China's silence signals limited buy-in; don't price in a meaningful US-China AI détente from this summit.
insights.locator: It’s clear Trump wants it to seem like discussions are going well.

insights.claim: People familiar with the AI alert plan said it is superficial because it involves no officials with technical expertise to assess the urgency of reported risks, a red flag also noted by CSET's Sam Bresnick.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
entities: Center for Security and Emerging Technology
insights.so_what: The mechanism is more diplomatic signaling than risk management.
insights.quote: the scientific, technical term is BS.
insights.locator: Notably, China has yet to publicly acknowledge the proposed alert system.

insights.claim: Omdia's Su Lian Jye says making the AI alert mechanism effective requires agreement on risk classifications, notification triggers, response protocols and review procedures, and it will not resolve disputes over distillation, pricing competition and pacing.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Commercial frictions (distillation, price competition) between US and Chinese AI labs persist regardless of safety talks.
insights.quote: I don’t think the dialog will remove all concerns and differences on distillation, pricing competition, and pacing

insights.claim: US-China AI tensions were heightened by expanding US export controls, congressional bills to cut China off from more chips and hardware, and a Justice Department accusation two weeks earlier that six leading Chinese AI makers stole from US frontier labs.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Escalating chip restrictions remain the base case, relevant to semiconductor exporters' China revenue.
insights.locator: However, the proposal comes at a time when China may not be ready

insights.claim: Stanford's Alvin Wang Graylin sees a follow-on US-China meeting scheduled for November as evidence both sides see value in AI dialogue.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: November meeting is a next catalyst for any easing of AI/tech tensions.
insights.locator: Graylin told Ars that he was surprised

insights.claim: Rep. Ro Khanna urged Trump to seek an international agreement banning recursive self-improving AI and safeguarding AI against misuse for biological and nuclear weapons.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Signals potential future regulatory constraints on frontier AI capabilities.

insights.claim: Sam Bresnick says China lacks the same public fear of AI because the state believes it can control AI, but expects US-China AI risk discussions to ramp up in six months to a year as Chinese capabilities catch up.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Watch for a shift in Chinese safety posture as its frontier models approach US capability.
insights.locator: Bresnick suggested that ongoing talks could be an opportunity

insights.claim: When the US or CEOs like Sam Altman push American-led global AI standards, China likely views 'AI safety' as a code word for suppressing Chinese AI and locking in US advantage, which could render the alert system useless.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Tying safety to dominance undermines cooperation, raising odds of fragmented AI standards.
insights.locator: When Trump or CEOs like Sam Altman advocate

insights.claim: Graylin says China regularly audits AI models and has knowledge from hundreds of audits to share, while the US has only just begun auditing AI, though the US has more experience auditing frontier models.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: China may be ahead in AI compliance/audit practice, relevant to AI assurance and audit service markets.
insights.locator: There’s much that the US and China can learn

insights.claim: Graylin argues there are at least two AI races, for intelligence and for market dominance: the US makes more money on frontier AI but is falling behind in the global race for users.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Frontier-model revenue leadership may not translate into global user share; track open-model adoption.
insights.locator: In reality, there are at least two races

insights.claim: Adoption of Chinese open AI models has exploded over the past six months, with Graylin predicting some may soon exceed 80 percent market share as CEOs cutting IT budgets choose cheaper, more data-private alternatives to frontier AI.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Price pressure on US frontier API providers from cheap open-weight Chinese models is a key margin risk.
insights.locator: In the last six months, adoption of China’s open models has exploded

insights.claim: Graylin writes that US-China frontier AI capability gaps typically last only a few months and no competitive moat will secure a permanent advantage for either nation.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Challenges the durable-lead thesis underpinning some Big Tech AI valuations and policy.
insights.quote: US-China capability gaps at the frontiers of AI technology typically last only a few months, and there is no competitive ‘moat’ that will secure a permanent advantage to either nation

insights.claim: US safety testing of frontier models delays deployment and gives rivals time to catch up, so even an artificial superintelligence lead could evaporate within weeks or months unless deployed untested.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: First-mover advantage in frontier AI may be structurally short-lived.
insights.locator: Further, US safety testing of frontier models delays access

insights.claim: Graylin argues the most dangerous AI models are often smaller specialized ones usable by non-state rogue actors for biological, chemical or cyber weapons, and that the assumed US-China conflict blocks cooperation against that threat.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Supports demand for cyber/biosecurity defenses irrespective of frontier-model race outcomes.
insights.quote: The most dangerous models are often those smaller specialized ones that could be created or utilized by non-state rogue actors

insights.claim: Graylin suggests Trump restore Biden's 'small yard' approach, narrowing export controls to genuine military and CBRNE threats rather than all advanced technology, which he says could let China deploy safer AI.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Any narrowing of export controls would be a positive catalyst for chipmakers' China sales, but article presents it as unlikely.

insights.claim: Graylin argues Trump's AI deregulation stance fuels domestic societal fear of AI that will hinder US economic deployment of the technology and reduce competitiveness, recommending reasonable safety regulation.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Public backlash is framed as an adoption risk for US AI; regulation could paradoxically aid deployment.
insights.locator: Additionally, Trump could consider following China’s lead

top_entities: Center for Security and Emerging Technology
